bibliographic.title: Concentration-Dependent Speciation in ZnCl2 Electrolyte Solutions: Transferability of Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials and Speciation Sensitivity of EXAFS

affiliations.text: Integrated Discovery Sciences Directorate, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, WA 99352, USA
X-ray Science Division, Argonne National Laboratory, Argonne, IL 60439, USA

bibliographic.abstract: Predicting speciation in concentrated electrolytes requires accurate ion interactions and sufficient sampling of slowly interconverting coordination environments. We combine Zn K-edge extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) measurements with long-timescale molecular dynamics (MD) driven by machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) to investigate aqueous ZnCl2 from dilute to 30 m. Using active learning, we train revPBE-based DeepMD potentials with D3 corrections included or excluded for Zn-containing pairs and compare them with DPMD-SCAN, classical MD (CMD), and MACE-MATPES-r2SCAN. We benchmark related EXAFS calculations against hydrated and chloride-coordinated Zn reference complexes, calculate spectra from MD ensembles, and examine Zn–Cl coordination free energies. Increasing concentration reduces octahedral Zn coordination, promotes replacement of water by chloride, and increases chloride-bridged association. Although all three DeepMD models yield similar EXAFS at 3 m, DPMD-SCAN shows greater transferability across concentrations, reproducing measured spectral trends, capturing key features of mixed ZnCl2/LiCl spectra, and predicting octahedral fractions consistent with other studies. DFT treatment strongly affects coordination free energies and aggregation, while excluding Zn-related D3 corrections does not systematically improve EXAFS agreement. CMD shows larger spectral discrepancies and less consistent coordination trends. MACE-MATPES-r2SCAN improves upon CMD and produces spectra comparable to DPMD-SCAN, but DPMD-SCAN provides more consistent agreement and greater computational efficiency. Neighbor-resolved analysis reveals that distance disorder and interference among scattering paths can produce similar EXAFS signatures for distinct coordination ensembles. This highlights the importance of rigorous molecular sampling and ensemble-averaged spectral calculations to complement EXAFS when interpreting isolated versus chloride-bridged Zn speciation.
